newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr weighed down by Japanese sales.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr weighed down by Japanese sales.

text.p: The Australian dollar looks set to extend its two month old downtrend after failing to fully recover from a fresh burst of Japanese selling offshore.

The bail-out was led by a securities house as part of a fundamental switch to other higher yielders and took it to a new 11-month low of US$0.7569. Corporate bids and the absence of Tokyo for a holiday saw some of the losses recouped but faltered short of the 76 cent level, pointing to further weakness ahead.
An upbeat set of domestic housing and lending data failed to lift the mood as Japanese investors were seen determined to sell no matter what the outlook for interest differentials.
By 4.45 (0545 GMT) the local dollar had stolen back to US$0.7583/88 from its offshore low at US$0.7564/69 but was still short on Monday's late US$0.7598/03.
The offshore lurch ended a week of consolidation and put paid to thoughts the currency may finally have found a floor in its sharp downtrend from December's six-year peak of US$0.8212.
They now looked for a drift to interim support at US$0.7550 and eventually the long standing bear target of 75 cents.
A near term break above 76 cents was needed to counter the bearish momentum and the distant US$0.7735 level would have to be cleared to signal a trend reversal.

The weight of Japanese sales had played a large part in this year's decline from atop 79 cents as falling yields in Australia contrasted with an upward trend in the U.S. and U.K. to turn the head of Japanese retail investors.

Not only had the flow of yen/A$ samurais dried up but the very weakness of the yen made it both attractive and profitable for Japanese investors to cut their long A$ positions built up last year when those samurais were all the rage.
Thus even though the A$ had slid over four percent on its U.S. counterpart this year, it was not far from 4-1/2 year highs on the yen at 93.33/43, steady on Monday's late 93.28/38.
The dollar was also firm on the mark at 1.2595/11 from 1.2518/38 as dismal German unemployment data released last week stirred speculation the Bundesbank may yet ease again.
That helped limit the dip on its trade weighted index to 58.0 from 58.1 on Monday.
But it continued to lose out to sterling and, to a lesser extent, the Canadian dollar as the next move in their rates was expected to be upwards.
In contrast, the outlook for Australian rates was more uncertain with analysts seeing a 50/50 chance the Reserve Bank would ease policy again in the next couple of months.
Many felt the odds lengthened somewhat last week when Q4 wages data proved more robust than expected, and today's figures contained nothing to change that view.

Housing finance commitments rose 5.3 percent in December to reverse a 2.9 percent drop the month before and top forecasts of a 4.0 percent gain. That was up 7.4 percent on the year and even when refinancing was excluded, commitments still rose a healthy 4.2 percent on the month.
Growth was also strong in value terms with total mortgages rising 6.6 percent to A$4.22 billion in December, the highest level since May 1994 and the fifth highest on record.
The upbeat message was echoed in private sector credit data for December which showed a 0.8 percent gain, with lending for housing up 0.9 percent and personal credit up 1.0 percent.
The RBA has long looked for a revival in the housing market in 1997 to contribute to a pick up in general economic growth, so should be encouraged by this data, analysts said.

"The figures helps confirm that the housing sector has edged out of its recent trough and is experiencing a gentle recovery," said John Peters, a senior economist at Westpac. "As such, it reinforces our view that the RBA will not ease again this cycle." -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
